component.name: Photo Vault
component.summary: Manage, search and develop photos on your own machine
Fotos auf dem eigenen Rechner verwalten, durchsuchen und entwickeln

description.p: Photo Vault keeps a photo library on the machine it runs on. Nothing is uploaded: importing, searching, face grouping, captioning and RAW development all happen locally.

Photo Vault verwaltet eine Fotobibliothek auf dem Rechner, auf dem es läuft. Nichts wird hochgeladen – Einlesen, Suchen, Gesichter gruppieren, Beschreiben und RAW-Entwicklung geschehen vollständig vor Ort.
Included:
Enthalten sind:

ul.li: Timeline, albums, map, calendar and people views
Zeitleiste, Alben, Karte, Kalender und Personen
Non-destructive RAW development with curves and masks
Zerstörungsfreie RAW-Entwicklung mit Kurven und Masken
Optional local AI models for search, captions, faces and text
Wahlweise lokale KI-Modelle für Suche, Beschreibungen, Gesichter und Text

description.p: AI models are not shipped with the application. They are downloaded on request from their public sources and can be removed again at any time.
Die KI-Modelle liegen der Anwendung nicht bei. Sie werden auf Wunsch aus ihren öffentlichen Quellen geladen und lassen sich jederzeit wieder entfernen.

Map tiles are fetched for the rounded zoom level, so a swipe across ten levels asked for ten full screens of tiles - measured 4252 loads for the ~150 that end up visible, with the one tile you want queued behind thousands nobody wants any more. Tile loading is now throttled to five times a second while zooming; panning is unchanged.

When a cached tile has expired and nobody answers, the tile already on disk is shown instead of a grey hole. This is what pre-loaded areas are for: they were worthless offline on day 31, although every tile was already there.

Three waits are gone: the result count in the filter bar (90.2 ms to 1.9 ms), the library health screen no longer waits for the storage figure (1372 ms warm, 2788 ms cold) before showing anything, and person suggestions no longer rebuild every person centroid on each tap (62 ms to 3.5 ms).

Face recognition was invisible where it was needed: on a grown library no face waits "open", so no suggestion and no card appeared - although 960 set-aside faces could be named today. They are now counted separately, with the run offered next to the number.

Face recognition now runs by itself after every import. Faces close enough to a named person are suggested, grouped per person and confirmed with one click - nothing is assigned automatically, because a wrong suggestion that someone overlooks costs a wrong assignment.
The memories section asks the next larger question when the calendar day has nothing: "in September, 13 years ago" instead of vanishing without a word.

Invented capture dates no longer appear as memories. Timestamps sitting on a full hour are treated as guessed - chance hits that twice per library, an import without a time of day hits it a thousand times.
The library health screen additionally reports waiting person suggestions, questionable capture dates and videos judged from a single frame.
Backup verification checks the manifest, file hashes and encrypted backup integrity before a restore is needed.
Similar photos can now be merged into one kept item while retaining albums, tags and the strongest metadata.
This release changes no data and no schema. It closes a gap at the one place where the app hands something out of the window: the video you pass on.

Altitude, speed and gradient have been under the terrain view since the flyover was built - as a row of widgets, below the picture. On screen that is the right place. A video has no "below": what leaves the app is the canvas and nothing else. Whoever shared a hike shared a pretty landscape with a camera flying along it, and not a single number. The numbers were there all along, one screen edge too far down - and they are exactly the reason anyone watches a flyover at all.

They now sit inside the picture, bottom left: above the attribution, below the middle, out of the way of the photo in the opposite corner. They fade in with the approach and out with the credits - what the flight is measuring right now has no business next to the numbers of the whole tour. Every measure scales with the picture height, so 1280x720 and 3840x2160 produce the same image.

Each slot is as wide as the widest form its value takes anywhere in this flight, computed once beforehand from two hundred samples along the route. A slot that grows with its content shifts everything to its right thirty times a second as soon as the speed goes from 9.9 to 10.1 km/h - and equal-width digits alone do not help, because it is the number of digits that changes, not their width. Uphill and downhill get fixed colours instead of the theme's: the theme's colours are made for the theme's background, while these numbers sit on a dark plate over changing landscape. The colour stays decoration - the sign says the same thing.
Cost per frame at 1920x1080: 18.94 ms instead of 18.51 ms, an extra 0.43 ms or 2.3 per cent.

Checked at the pixels, twice: on the painter alone, and on the actually exported video, whose raw pixels a stand-in ffmpeg catches. A value that is computed and passed along is not thereby drawn - the progress bar of the video export was computed, handed to the flight bar and painted nowhere for four weeks.
Also: the Windows build script now collects companion libraries in rounds and aborts if one is missing, instead of quietly shipping a package in which a tool does not start.

This release builds no new feature. It makes the existing data more accurate - starting with the app no longer asserting something that is not true. Schema 73 to 78; the migration runs at first start and is not reversible, nothing is lost.

1,097 of 7,443 photos carry a timestamp on a full hour - no minutes, no seconds. Chance would predict two. 948 of them carry the very same instant to the second. The files say "DateTimeOriginal: 0000:00:00 00:00:00": the camera clock was never set, and the import fell back to the file system timestamp. That fallback is correct and named as a last resort in the source; what was wrong was the silence afterwards. The guessed value sat in the same column as a measured one, so the timeline put half a childhood on a single evening, memories claimed "20 years ago today" for 948 photos that were not taken that day, and burst detection found a "burst" with 943 members. An estimated date now says so, stays out of memories and bursts, and can be found and corrected in one go. The mark itself is not guessed: instead of one line of SQL over everything that sits on a full hour, a pass looks inside every file.

547 photos can inherit a place from their neighbours in time. The same calculation was measured and rejected four days ago at 68 hits; since then 246 videos got their place from the file and 228 photos got one by hand. A rejected measurement only holds for the data it was taken on. The value lies in staying silent: it counts whether ALL neighbours in the window were at the same spot - 35 of 582 candidates drop out, and those are exactly the ones that would have been wrong. Offered as a suggestion with its reasoning, and an accepted place stays marked as inherited.

A video is no longer a single still frame. 428 of 429 videos had an embedding, tags and faces - all from one image taken half a second in. For a two-second live photo that is the whole video; for the nine-minute one it is a sample of 0.2 per mille. From ten seconds of runtime, up to five frames spread over the length are analysed. The frames are not kept. In search the best frame counts, not their average - an average across different scenes is a vector that no longer fits anything.

Sentence search reaches three more fields: sharpness, ISO and date provenance. Aperture and focal length stay out on purpose - "aperture 2.8" does not settle whether exactly 2.8 or "at least this open" is meant, and a half-understood value is worse than none.

1,016 photos carry a time-zone offset in the file that the app never read. It is now read in the same pass that looks at where the date came from. The capture time itself is untouched: it is the camera's local time, and that is the time one remembers. A written "+00:00" is not believed - all 131 occurrences come from one Canon EOS R10, 34 of them located in Germany and the rest from November and December between 04:32 and 18:56. Germany is never UTC+0; the value is a factory default.
A follow-up with a single point: the flyover video export works on macOS. In 3.5.0 it did not, and the advice the app gave along the way was wrong. No schema change - the database stays at 73.

3.5.0 said video export needed a separately installed ffmpeg and would find it by itself afterwards. Neither was true, and anyone who followed the advice got the same message again. Measured with a purpose-signed probe bundle carrying exactly the app's entitlements, launched once from a command line and once from the Finder: stat() on /opt/homebrew/bin/ffmpeg succeeds in both cases, while access(X_OK) and posix_spawn fail with EPERM in both. Two independent reasons, either of which would have been enough on its own: the sandbox does not let the app start a foreign program - the tool search would even have found ffmpeg, it just could never have run it - and an app launched from the Dock does not have Homebrew on its PATH at all, only four system directories. The second reason is why this went unnoticed: launched through "open" from a terminal the app inherits the full PATH, so every check made from a command line sees something different from what the user sees.

macOS now writes the video itself. AVFoundation is part of the system, runs inside the sandbox, encodes through VideoToolbox in hardware and carries no GPL obligation. Linux and Windows keep the bundled ffmpeg, where it sits in the package and can actually be started. Measured at 90 frames of 1920 by 1080: 0.3 seconds through AVFoundation against 4.4 through ffmpeg. The file is larger on the native path because VideoToolbox encodes to a fixed data rate rather than a quality level; the rate is derived from the frame area and lands where ffmpeg does at -crf 20 for 1080p30.

Verified in three places, because none of them alone would do. A method channel leads nowhere in a unit test, and the sandbox at the heart of this is not there at all - which is exactly the gap the fault lived in. A test rig cuts the Swift class verbatim out of the shipped file, compiles it on its own and has ffprobe read the result, plus a colour check on real pixels: swapped red and blue would produce a perfectly playable video that no probe field says anything about. Thirteen tests against a stubbed channel check the seam. And one test runs inside the live, sandboxed application, where ffmpeg is findable and yet unstartable, and AVFoundation reads the freshly written file back at 2.00 seconds.

The flyover across an activity used to be a hiking map at an angle. It is now an aerial map on which the path is actually visible - with trails, place names, contour lines, named peaks, your own photos at the spot where they were taken, and a video to pass on. Database schema changes from 71 to 73; the migration runs on first start and is not reversible.

Why it was blurry: map image and elevation grid shared one zoom limit and one tile budget, which picked zoom 14 for a 2.8 by 3.3 km walk - 5.90 metres per pixel. The foreground carried a huge smeared "643.2", a zoom-14 label magnified sixteen times. The elevation data has to stop at zoom 15 because the source offers nothing beyond it; the texture does not - but it cannot simply jump to 18 either, because 270 MB in a single image surface can neither be held nor even created.

So the landscape now falls into about a hundred blocks along the tile boundaries. Each carries its own texture and picks its own zoom by distance from the camera: sharp nearby, coarse in the distance, and only what is actually in frame gets fetched - a twelve kilometre flight touches over a thousand blocks. The mesh underneath is aligned to the block boundaries rather than spread evenly, otherwise a cell would straddle an edge and the last pixel of the block image would be stretched along it. What lies behind the camera is not drawn at all: each block is its own draw call, and at equal triangle counts six blocks cost 1.27 ms per frame against 7.02 ms for nine hundred - 1.07 against 4.35 ms with the visibility check.

Aerial imagery is now the default. That is a visible change for everyone and it is deliberate: a hiking map answers "what was this path called", an aerial image answers "what did it look like there", and that is the question a flyover is watched for. The map menu switches back, and the layers on top - trails, roads and place names, contour lines, peaks and huts - are switchable one by one. And the aerial image alone would not do: checked against the real tile of the Ilse valley it shows dense forest, and the path the walk followed is not visible on it. Only the trail layer makes it appear. Each layer has its own ceiling, set not only by what the provider serves but by what may reasonably be asked of it - Waymarked Trails is run by volunteers and stays at zoom 16 although the service goes to 18. Measured on the same extent: OpenTopoMap delivered 31 of 88 blocks in 120 seconds, Esri 88 of 88 in 10.

Contour lines are computed rather than fetched. They come out of the same grid the landscape is built from, so they cannot sit beside the slope they describe, they stay sharp at every zoom, and they cost not a single request.

Peaks, huts and springs stand upright above the terrain instead of lying flat on it. They come from OpenStreetMap, with the surveyed elevation where one is recorded. They do not shine through mountains - the view has no depth buffer, so the line of sight is sampled for every sign - and they do not cover each other: whoever stands closer wins, and never more than twelve names are shown. What has been queried once stays in the library; Overpass is run by volunteers, and a tour looked at a second time asks nobody.

The flight now opens with an approach from the overview onto the starting point, shows each photo as it passes the spot where it was taken, and closes with the numbers of the tour as the camera pulls back up. Ascent counts only what goes up: the plain difference between start and finish says zero for a round trip, however far one climbed.

And it can be written out as an MP4 at 1920 by 1080, with photos, contour lines, signs and the attribution of the map sources burned in - that is a licence requirement, not decoration. Measured on a real run: 90 frames in 4.4 seconds. On macOS the export needs a separately installed ffmpeg; on Linux and Windows it is bundled. If it is missing, the app says so instead of quietly doing nothing.

One fault that had been there all along: the landscape is drawn from triangles without a depth buffer, and the view relied on the grid order - north to south - already running back to front. That only holds while the camera looks north, and the flight camera turns with the direction of travel. Walking south showed distant terrain painted over near terrain: a broad band across the landscape, 960 of 3120 sampled pixels. It never showed because the imaging tool always flew northwards. Every frame is now sorted by depth, at a cost of two percent of a frame.

A follow-up without new features. It started with one open question - whether Flutter's default image cache is large enough - and three faults fell out of measuring it. All three sit in the timeline, the most used screen. No schema change: the database stays at 71.

Square tiles showed their photos squashed. A tile limits the size a thumbnail is decoded to, and both edges were given - but that does not mean "at most this large" to Flutter, it means "exactly this size", and the aspect ratio is not preserved. A 225x400 portrait became a 225x320 bitmap. The crop notices nothing: it receives an image whose ratio is already wrong and dutifully fills the tile, so faces came out wider and flatter without anything looking like an error. It only became visible in a test image containing circles, which came out as ellipses. Affected were the timeline, the photo markers on the map and the filmstrip under the viewer. Exactly one edge is given now.

Every month decoded a photo nobody saw. The timeline lays out each month as its own section, and a section always builds its first element - even one entirely below the window, because its height has to be known. That first element was a photo, so opening the timeline decoded the first photo of every single month down to the oldest: 581 images for a screen showing 69. The month heading is now that first element instead, and it costs no image. The timeline appears in less than half the time.

The scrubber jumped too far down. The calculation behind the scrubber and "jump to this photo" assumed a month heading of 64 points where 52 are drawn, plus a gap after the last row of a square grid that does not exist. Twelve points per month add up: in the middle of a library with 82 months the jump landed 668 points too low, two thirds of a window height. It is exact now.

And the image cache itself: Flutter's default of 100 MB holds barely three screenfuls of the timeline on a high resolution display, so scrolling back showed empty tiles refilling. It is 200 MB now, measured to cover seven to ten screens. 300 MB was rejected - the first extra hundred megabytes buy four screens, the second hundred also only four.

Three wishes and one fault found while checking them. Database schema changes from 68 to 71 - the migration runs on first start and is not reversible; verified against three grown libraries, one of them at version 27.

The timeline can now show photos in their own aspect ratio instead of cropped squares, every row filled exactly to the full width. Rows and not a column wall: in a timeline sorted by date the second photo belongs beside the first, not below it. A button in the header switches between the two forms and the choice is remembered. A side effect is a more accurate scrubber - with squares the height of a month group was an estimate, with rows it is calculated. The image cache was the stated risk and was measured rather than assumed: 17.8 against 16.5 MB per screenful at the default step, and at the largest step rows are actually cheaper.

Videos and live photos start playing when the mouse rests on them for a moment - muted, looping, until the pointer moves on. The delay matters: without it a pointer sweeping across the wall would drag a trail of starting videos behind it. Only one ever plays, because each playback is its own mpv process. Locked items stay still: playing them would mean decrypting them in passing. It can be switched off under Settings, Appearance.

The terrain flight gets a sky gradient instead of the theme background, aerial haze into the distance, a soft edge where the loaded data ends, the track drawn in three passes (offset shadow, soft glow, sharp core), and a time of day - morning, midday, evening, blue hour - switchable in the header and remembered. Midday keeps exactly the previous lighting. The sun stays in the north-west at every time of day: a surface lit from the lower right reads as a hollow, so lighting a morning from the east would turn every valley into a hill. What moves is the sun's height, and with it the length of the shadows.

And the fault: migration steps were ordered descending from number 48 onwards. For a library at version 54 or later this never showed, because the affected steps no longer run there. An older one could not be opened at all - step 65 writes into a table that step 54 creates, so the migration aborted with "no such table" and the app with it. Found because the migration test took on a library at version 27 that happened to be lying around. Fixed by reordering; a test now holds the order in place.

A Windows follow-up, and a more necessary one than expected: the released 3.3.0 does not start at all on a clean Windows. macOS and Linux are unaffected and change only in the version number. No schema change - the database stays at 68.

Unpacking 3.3.0 on a fresh Windows and clicking photo_vault.exe gives no window but a system error: "The code execution cannot proceed because MSVCP140.dll was not found." The Visual C++ runtime was missing from the package. Eleven files need it, among them onnxruntime.dll - so every AI feature - and libraw.dll for RAW. The fault is in every Windows release so far. It was never noticed because there was never a clean test machine: the build machine has the runtime from Visual Studio, and so does the Windows test machine. Only the Windows Sandbox, a genuinely untouched system, revealed it. The four files now ship with the package, and the build reads the import tables of every executable in it, flagging whatever is required but absent.

The same check found zlib.dll - 203 kB from the ANGLE set that Flutter ships, and a debug build requiring vcruntime140d.dll and ucrtbased.dll, neither of which may be redistributed nor exists on any user machine. No file in the package imports it, and the app loaded 94 modules without it. It is gone.

New: an MSIX package for the Microsoft Store, built by tool\windows_msix.ps1 from the finished package folder. Store-delivered packages bypass Smart App Control entirely because Microsoft re-signs them - the only route that really resolves the block described in 3.3.0. Verified in the sandbox: installed in 6.4 seconds, full user interface, ONNX Runtime loaded, and the bundled tools run from the install folder - ffmpeg writes an image, heif-dec decodes a HEIC sample to 1200 by 800. The zip stays alongside it for direct downloads.

Anyone moving from the zip to the packaged build keeps their library. Windows reports a different data folder to a packaged app, so without a fallback the app would come up empty while the library sat unreachable beside it. Nothing is moved, though: measured in the sandbox, a packaged process may read and write the old location and both pass through to the real place - only what goes through SHGetKnownFolderPath is redirected. The packaged build therefore simply keeps using what is already there, at no cost and with no model re-downloaded. Only where nothing exists - a fresh Store install - does it use the package folder.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemawechsel.
The largest release since 3.0.0: twenty-seven items from two rounds of wishes, plus the 23rd audit. Database schema changes from 66 to 68 - the migration runs on first start and is not reversible.

First, a repair that came from no wish list: the AI search had been dead for a month. Both CLIP encoders shipped in half precision since 30 August, and the bundled ONNX Runtime 1.23.0 simply cannot open them - a search returned nothing at all rather than few results. The uncomfortable part is why nobody noticed: the probe read the models from the test build's container, where the old files still sat, so every check since the switch had verified a model the app does not ship. There is now a test that really opens both encoders and makes them compute.

Developing: six sliders moved without changing the picture. Sharpening, noise reduction, clarity and vignetting cannot be done by the fast preview at all, and white balance only approximately, so they waited until you let go - as did every slider of a mask. The exact render now runs while you drag, 42 ms on a 24-megapixel photo, with no fixed rate: only one pass runs at a time and whatever accumulates is folded into a single follow-up. The history used to appear only on saving; every settled state is now recorded, and each entry says what was done, not just when. AI restoration reports its progress where you started it, with time remaining and a cancel button. And the preview really is new after saving - editing writes the rotated image to the same path, and Flutter remembers decoded images by path.

Timeline: five tile sizes instead of one, and the list view gets eleven selectable columns with names, draggable widths and check marks in the menu. Previously five fixed ones without headings, whose visibility depended solely on window width. In a narrow window nothing silently drops out any more; the list scrolls sideways.
Overview: empty sections are gone, the strips now fill the screen instead of showing a fixed number of tiles, and activities finally appear there at all.

Map: the tile store and the display no longer spoke the same language - since 3.1.1 the map requests server level z+1 for display level z, while the store still loaded 3 to 14. Zooming to level 14 meant waiting on the network despite a full store. A new switch turns the doubled resolution off, because the sharpness costs 2.6 times as many tiles per screen. The calendar gains a month level, the terrain takes the remembered map style instead of always OpenTopoMap, and the camera flight follows a smoothed look-at point (mean jerk 2.83 down to 0.08 m).
Family tree: separated parents are two households, but the mesh carried only one parent house per person and stopped after the first, so the father stood in the picture without any connection.

The 23rd audit: locking a photo left the plaintext in the image cache; the decryption cache had no upper bound; several labels overflowed at large system font sizes; and grey small text was unreadable in the light theme at 2.07:1 where 4.5:1 is required.

Known limitation on Windows, not affecting Linux or macOS: where Smart App Control enforces, the application does not start at all - blocked on all three launch paths with "blocked by the Device Guard policy of your organisation", logged as CodeIntegrity 3077/3118 naming photo_vault.exe. Not a fault of this release: 2.7.0 and 2.7.1 still run on the same machine because they were there before Windows switched Smart App Control from evaluation to enforcement, and the released 3.2.0 archive fails the same way when freshly unpacked. Nor is it the age of the file - a copy of 2.7.1 written just now runs fine with the same checksum. What sets a newly published release apart is a checksum nobody has ever seen: an unsigned program without reputation is refused. The way out is a signature, not a change to the packaging. Separately, ffmpeg and heif-dec also fail at DLL load time (0xC0000142), which would leave video previews empty and HEIC photos invisible; statically linked tools remain the measured remedy for that half. Smart App Control is only active on freshly installed Windows 11 and usually stays in evaluation; where it enforces it can be switched off, but only once and never back on without reinstalling Windows.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek - aber diesmal mit Schemawechsel von 66 auf 68.

The overview of map sources said which map goes deepest - and then left you to copy the address template out by hand. Every row now has its buttons. No database change - version 66 stays, updating is a plain program swap.

Three buttons, depending on the row. The bundled maps (light, dark, topography) can be made the default view. A template without a key can be switched on with one click: notice, on, default, in one go - that covers both Esri maps, OpenStreetMap Germany and CyclOSM, where address, attribution and zoom limit are all present and nothing is missing that anyone would have to obtain. Mapbox, MapTiler, Thunderforest and Google Maps stay with the form below, because their address carries the key marker; switched on with a single click the provider would answer with a permission error, and on screen that looks like a broken map. Whichever view is currently remembered carries a mark in its title and no longer has a button - having nothing to do is information too.

And a link to every provider, the three bundled ones included, where it points at openstreetmap.org/copyright, carto.com and opentopomap.org. That was the actual break: the notice before switching on a third-party source says that the provider's terms apply and that the app cannot take that off anyone's hands. That sentence is only honest if the terms can actually be reached without typing the name out first. In the form, "keys are available from ..." became a button for the same reason.

Only what begins with http or https and has a host is opened. The value ends up as the argument of a system command, and "open" on macOS starts programs too - a file: scheme or a path to an application bundle would be something other than opening a page. The addresses do come from a bundled list, but lists like that grow.

The chain is now complete: take it, make it the default, fill the store. The pre-load further down in the same settings has always followed the remembered view, the custom source included - so anyone who takes Esri World Imagery and then pre-loads fills the store with Esri tiles and not with the dark ones. What is new is only that a sentence above the buttons says so.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemawechsel.

A follow-up with a single cause: on a display with double pixel density the map only ever drew half the resolution. Anyone on a MacBook, a Retina display or a 4K screen will see the difference at once. No database change - version 66 stays, updating is a plain program swap.

The zoom was never the problem. It was reported that the dark map and the topographic map could not be zoomed to street level. Measured across all four ways in, each reaches its stop: dark 6 to 21, topo 6 to 19. And the map screen, zoomed in step by step and written out as an image, shows street names, shop names and house numbers at level 19. So the tiles were arriving and the map went as deep as it should.

What was missing was resolution. A tile is 256 pixels wide and is drawn onto 256 points. On a display with double pixel density that is 512 device points - each tile pixel covers four of them. The map was therefore as coarse at every level as it should have been one level higher, and that reads exactly like "street level is not possible".

The map library has always been able to do better and expressly recommends it for high pixel densities; it had simply never been switched on. Where the tile address contains an "{r}" placeholder (CARTO, Mapbox, MapTiler) the double-resolution tiles come straight from the server. Otherwise four tiles of the next deeper level are fetched and placed where one would go: the same area, four times the pixels. Measured on real tiles over Hannover, mean neighbour difference at pixel density 2: topo z16 goes from 11.70 to 44.27, OSM z16 from 5.31 to 9.57. Looking at the images says more than the number - at topo level 16 house numbers, building outlines and shop names appear that simply were not there before.

Once the measurement had to be overruled. At OSM level 18 the figure FELL, from 4.38 to 3.37, and the image still carried more content: finer lettering has less contrast per pixel, and a sharpness measure that counts neighbour differences penalises that. The decision was therefore made from the images.

One wrong turn, so nobody repeats it: with simulated double resolution the map library lowers the highest native level by one and adds a zoom offset to the address instead. Raising that number to compensate makes the app request tiles that do not exist - OpenStreetMap returns an error from level 20 on. The number that matters is the sum of the two.

Until now map depth could only be discussed in zoom levels, and "up to level 17" means nothing to anyone. Hence two additions: a scale bar at the bottom left of the map, and an overview of all map sources under Settings - Map, giving for each source its depth in levels AND in metres, whether that figure was measured or is claimed by the provider, whether a key is needed, whether double resolution comes from the server or is simulated, and the attribution. A hundred screen points at mid latitudes: z14 588 m, z15 294 m, z16 147 m, z17 74 m, z19 18 m, z20 9 m.

The price: smaller lettering - which is how every native map app looks - more tile requests, and offline the pre-loaded store reaches one display level less deep, since it holds server levels 3 to 14 and those now serve display levels 2 to 13.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemawechsel.

The map stayed grey, and the reason was not the one it looked like. Plus a map source of your own for anyone OpenStreetMap does not reach deep enough for, and a way to take photographs out of a journey or an activity that can actually be found. Database change to version 66 - five new columns in the settings, nothing else.

The grey map was not the servers. Measured before anything was changed, 36 tiles in one go through the app's real client: OSM z12 121 ms, z16 122 ms, z19 113 ms, Topo z12 240 ms, z17 143 ms - all 200. Street level was never barred either. What made it look barred sat in the tile store: 29,819 tiles, topography complete to level 14 from pre-loading, OpenStreetMap only to level 10 from browsing. Only what lay in the store was drawn; everything beyond it stayed grey.

There was not a single deadline anywhere in the tile path - neither on connecting nor on waiting for the answer. Together with the cap of six connections per server that is enough: if six answers fail to arrive - half-open connections after sleep, a network change, or a server that accepts and says nothing - every further request waits for a slot that never frees up. Reproduced against a silent server: after 2 s six connections open and no request finished, after 10 s the seventh still not finished. And the real catch is that this seventh request never FAILS, it waits. So the map library reports no failed tile either, and the follow-up ladder of 5, 15 and 45 seconds never starts - there is no error for it to hang on.

connectionTimeout is the wrong lever for this, and that was the first attempt: the connection does stand, it is accepted, only nothing comes back. Measured in the same experiment: with a one-second connection deadline, not one of eight requests aborted within twenty seconds. There is now a fifteen-second deadline on the ANSWER, and it really tears the connection down. Ten requests against the same silent server all return as failures after three seconds - and with that the ladder that already existed takes over. The map's own abort for tiles that scroll out of view is untouched and is still not retried.

Second fault on the same screen: whatever failed once stayed gone offline. The tile layer appends a fragment to the address of a failed tile so the library requests it again. Invisible to the server - but not to the tile store on disk, whose key is a UUID over the full address. A tile that had failed once was never looked for on disk again, so without a network the hole stayed even though the pre-loaded image was long since in the house - precisely the situation pre-loading exists for.

A map source of your own. The bundled maps stop early: OpenStreetMap serves real tiles to level 19, OpenTopoMap to 17. Under Settings - Map you can now enter your own source: address, attribution, zoom limit. It appears as a fourth entry in the map menu and is served by pre-loading like the others. A URL template rather than a list of providers in the program, because every provider hangs its key somewhere else. Templates are included; the zoom limits of the key-free ones are measured against real requests. Esri repeats the OpenTopoMap trap: above level 20 it answers with status 200 and the same 2,521-byte substitute tile - a status code of 200 and still no map. Each template therefore states whether its level was measured or taken from the provider's documentation.

Before switching a third-party source on there is a notice in three parts. Data transmission: every tile is a request to that provider, revealing which part of the world is being looked at, how far in, and for how long - with the bundled maps the other end is a donated server without an account, here it is a key issued to you. Offline: tiles you have looked at stay on disk and pre-loading whole areas works here too, but anything never looked at stays grey. And the terms: how far a provider permits caching is set out in its conditions - some for a limited time, some not at all, and Google explicitly forbids offline use, which is exactly what this app does.

Taking photographs out of a journey or an activity. The route existed - a button in the title bar opening a grid with ticks. It was not found. It carried a library symbol, because it also REMOVES photographs and a plus sign does not say that, and so it stood as the seventh of seven symbols and was read as "add photographs", and therefore never looked for. Removing now has its own route: tap photographs in the grid, a bar at the bottom, "remove from journey". Which lets the button in the title bar carry a plus sign and mean what it says. Removing is not deleting: the photograph stays in the library, it simply no longer belongs to that outing.

A follow-up: five faults and one round of optimisation, all found the day after 3.0.0. No database change - version 65 stays, updating is a plain program swap. One of the faults cost data, so anyone running 3.0.0 should move on.

The photographs of an activity could not be changed, and a single tick deleted the rest. On saving, the assignment table is emptied and rewritten with exactly the returned set - but that set was built from the screen's DISPLAY LIST, and that list differs from the assignment in two places. It filters out whatever sits in the trash or the locked folder: in a grown library 33 journey assignments pointed at such photographs, and pressing Done WITHOUT ANY CHANGE would have deleted them. And it is empty while the screen is still loading, because the loading guard covered only the body and not the buttons in the title bar - tap "edit photographs" quickly enough and you get a screen without a single tick although the activity has photographs. One tick on that, and the others were gone, reported as "1 added, 0 removed". The starting set now comes straight from the database, without a join and without a filter, and the title-bar buttons appear only once loading is done. Tapping itself was never broken.

The duplicate search missed half of them. Both searches ran through the same pre-filter: two random projections with a window of 200. Held against a complete all-against-all run on a grown library (7475 embeddings, 9.2 s for the truth), counting GROUPS as one sees them: 21 of 42 groups before, 41 of 42 now, for a quarter more computing time. The comment at that spot called the chance of missing a pair "negligible in practice". It was not. For SERIES the projection was the wrong road altogether: a series demands at most 30 seconds between two shots anyway, and that condition is exact rather than estimated - it merely stood behind the expensive comparison instead of in front of it. 512 instead of 324 groups, and faster: 153 instead of 227 ms. You will see both - noticeably more duplicate groups and more series suggestions than before.

Explore jumped back to the top by itself. Whoever scrolled down to the trash and then wanted to go back a little stood at the beginning again after two small drags. The page was a lazy list whose sections differ greatly in height, and at the bottom such a list estimates its total height from the short sections currently laid out: a drag of 120 points moved the page by 950.

Grey map tiles stayed grey. The tile layer follows up after a failure - after 5, 15 and 45 seconds. Only the first step was ever reached: Flutter attaches its listener only when the image key has changed, and the round counter deliberately appeared in no address. So there was exactly one second attempt and never another; whatever was missing after five seconds was missing until the program closed.

Less fetched where less will do. The trash figure pulled 618 full rows across the isolate boundary in order to count them; the database now does the counting, 13.0 instead of 0.3 ms, and that matters because this build runs on every notification of the library state. Duplicate and series suggestions issued one query per group: 52.2 instead of 12.6 ms at 324 groups.

Nine changes that all circle the same question: is what stands there true, and how long does it take to stand there. Database change to version 65.

Only one app per library. Two versions ran side by side on the Windows test machine for hours without either noticing. The app now claims the library BEFORE it opens the database - an operating-system lock on a file inside the library folder, not on the program, so two different libraries side by side stay possible and the same one twice does not. Whoever meets that sees a screen with three ways out rather than a crash.

Text recognition now reads what is actually there. Outside macOS the reading ran on a model from 2022. Measured against the shipped file, 96 samples of 16 German lines in three typefaces and two sizes: the old one got 95.5 percent and 25 of 96 lines faultless, the new one 99.7 percent and 90 of 96 - and it is SMALLER, 8.0 instead of 9.0 MB. The percentages are the dull part. The old model turned every sharp s into a B, thirty-nine times in 96 lines. The detection model stays as it was; both were measured at 0, 5 and 12 degrees of tilt and both find all eight lines.

Assigning people no longer means scrolling. The picker was a dropdown without search - 39 people as a list of thumbnails. Now typing filters an open list and the same button creates a person when nothing matches. And the suggestion existed all along and simply never arrived: of nine places where a face gets assigned, two filled it in, and the common paths were not among them.
Faces can be added in the full-screen view. Previously an overlooked face meant reopening the picture in a different screen.

The video half of a Live Photo is not a photograph of its own. Everywhere in the app that already held; in the travel and activity detection it did not, in the only two queries of ten that lacked it. What gets confirmed is what the timeline shows - the photographs. The video halves stayed behind, carried the same second and the same place, and gathered into a NEW suggestion for the same outing. In a grown library all three open suggestions were shadows of trips already confirmed, and the damage was already in the data: 19 activity and 7 journey assignments pointed at a video half, two activities consisted of seven video clips and no photograph at all. Version 65 bends every such assignment back to its photograph.

German country names. The country directory comes from GeoNames, which lists every country in English only, so the German interface said "Germany", "Poland", "Switzerland" - in the country list, on every photograph's info sheet, in the search filter, on the world map. The names now come from CLDR, the same data set operating systems use. Sorting and searching follow the displayed name, searching additionally the English one. In the database the English name stays: it is the key by which photograph and directory find each other.

A location can be undone again. An Olympus TG-810 filed thirty-one photographs in Afghanistan in 2013 - not a reading error, exiftool reads exactly the same coordinates with GPS status A, while the other 128 pictures from that camera carry status V and empty coordinates. No application can help with that. What it can help with is correcting it: setting a location used to write only the coordinates, the spelled-out names stayed, and because the backfill only fills rows without any country at all they stayed forever. Now they fall with the coordinate and are written afresh, and a whole selection can have its location REMOVED, not just set.

It got faster. Measured on a grown library of 7341 photographs. A data stream was thrown away on every rebuild: a call like watchTimeline returns a new object each time, and standing directly at a StreamBuilder it made that builder drop its subscription and open a new one on every rebuild - which runs the query afresh even while an identical one is still open next to it. In the timeline every arrow key and every click in a multiple selection does that, and after scrolling one of them cost 35.9 ms. A background run brought the interface to a halt: 200 single writes took 41.9 seconds with the timeline open on the whole library, and now take 0.5. And a join fetches every column of every table involved, including the ones nobody looks at - all image embeddings went from 105.0 to 19.3 ms, "On this day" from 253.2 to 32.6 ms.

One line, and the reason it matters. The database gave up the moment it met a lock. No database change.

SQLite's default for busy_timeout is zero: whoever meets a locked file gets "database is locked" at once and no second attempt. That stays harmless exactly as long as a single process touches the file - and nothing guarantees that. A backup service, a synchronised folder, a look with the sqlite3 tool, or simply the program started twice all hold the same lock. Measured with two processes each writing 400 rows at the same time: without a wait 734 of 800 writes fail; with five seconds none of them fail, and the whole thing takes 170 ms. The wait is affordable because the database is opened on a background isolate - it is not the interface that waits.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemaschritt.
A camera flight along an imported GPX track, three findings from an audit round, and CLIP at half the size. No database change.

The terrain view has always drawn the track as a line in space, but the camera stood still: to see how a path runs you had to turn it with the mouse. Now the camera follows the track and says where you are, how high, how fast and how steep. The path is sampled by METRES, not by points - a GPX file records densely where somebody was slow, so running the progress over the index would crawl through the village and shoot along the straight. Heading, speed and gradient come from a window of 120 metres, because two consecutive points lie as far apart as the accuracy of the device, and a speed taken from those jumps between 0 and 20 km/h. Below the picture an elevation profile runs along, filled up to the point the flight has reached; dragging it seeks.

Three faults that only the picture revealed. Triangles behind the camera drew streaks, because the projection puts them in the centre of the image - right for a line, ruinous for a triangle mesh, and never visible in the overview where the camera always stands outside the landscape. The camera distance now follows the MESH SPACING rather than the length of the track: at 96 cells over nine kilometres a cell is 94 metres wide, and from 480 metres away it covers 176 pixels, so the picture consisted of three grey surfaces. And the tilt was documented the wrong way round, which made the first version of the flight look like a tilted map.

A move used to leave the sidecar behind. Every photograph can carry an .xmp file next to it - description, keywords, rating, people, place, all in plain text. It is the only derived file that sits beside the original, and the move renamed only the original. In a grown library 1,244 of 7,370 sidecars lay where their photograph no longer was, and because the shared file list names the new path, such a file was neither encrypted when locking nor removed when deleting. Both are fixed, and the task "Sort files by date" now collects what was left behind.

Model files are checked again, not just once. The catalogue justifies its SHA-256 sums by the fact that the files are loaded straight into inference, yet the check happened only while downloading; afterwards the sole question was whether the file existed. The expected length is now compared at every glance, and a button in the settings recomputes every checksum for the case only that finds: right length, wrong content.

CLIP now runs in half precision - 606 MB become 303 MB. Measured on 600 real photographs: the eight-bit version saves more and is unusable (it halves what the duplicate search finds and changes the search results), half precision changes nothing at all and leaves the stored embeddings valid. SlimSAM was measured for the object masks and rejected: seven times smaller and four times faster, but its edges fray, and these masks carry local adjustments where an edge shows.
The trash now states how much it holds. In a grown library that was 619 shots and 6.01 GB - seven percent of everything, and neither the screen nor the settings said a word.
Capture dates for videos, and two background tasks that finally do what their card promises. The database moves from version 61 to 64; the migration runs by itself on first start.

Not one of 440 videos carried the right capture date. 309 of them hold one inside the file - it simply never arrived. The cause was not a reader that got it wrong but no reader at all: the EXIF library reads TIFF and JPEG, not MOV and MP4, so the import fell back on the file timestamp, which after every copy, backup and restore is the moment of that operation. 166 videos were off by more than a day, the oldest by twelve years. A reader now walks the container for three storage places: Apple's creationdate key with its time zone, the classic day atom, and the movie header. The time zone is the whole point - the movie header is supposed to hold UTC and Apple obeys, but measured against 28 videos carrying a GPS time as an incorruptible referee, it held local time throughout. So it is read as local time, and the program states whether a date is exact to the second or only to the zone offset. Checked against exiftool on 440 real files: 309 of 309 correct.

The task that should have fixed this did not look at videos. "Read capture date" asked for RAW photographs only; the same for camera data, which asked for images and thereby left 275 videos with maker and model in the file untouched while reading 842 photographs that provably carry none. Both now cover videos.

A date set by hand takes the file with it. Setting a date from the info panel or the batch dialog wrote only the column - the file stayed in the folder of the old month. In a grown library that affected 1,102 of 7,988 shots. Nothing looks wrong inside the program, which always follows the recorded path; it shows to whoever opens the library in a file manager or restores a backup. Both ways now move the file, and a new task with a confirmation puts the existing ones in order without touching a single date.

"Read places" remembers where it has looked. The task took every shot without coordinates - 5,756 of 7,988 - and read each file completely to look at the EXIF data. Measured on 400 of them: 3.3 seconds and 1,215 MB for zero hits, and again on the next run, because an unsuccessful look left no trace. A new column records it. The first run after the upgrade still goes over everything once and finds the 246 video locations it could never reach before; after that it is quiet. An "All" button remains for files given coordinates outside the program.

Also fixed: the face scan marked a photograph as scanned even when it could not be decoded at all, after which "missing only" passed it by forever. Zero cases in the test library - the fault was there, the damage was not.

Six points from the comparison with neighbouring programs - and the most important one did not come from the comparison but from the library itself. The database moves from version 59 to 61; the migration runs by itself on first start.

Rating without two hundred clicks. Ratings and colour labels have existed for many versions. Counting them in a grown library of 7,988 shots gave zero ratings and zero colour labels. The reason was not the feature but the way to it: the grid knew no key at all, selection began with a long press - a finger gesture - and there was no range selection whatsoever. Now: Shift-click takes in everything between the last clicked tile and the new one; Ctrl- or Command-click toggles a single tile; the arrow keys move a visible frame through the grid and Shift+arrow drags the selection along; 0-5 sets the rating, 6-9 the colour label, F the favourite, Escape clears, Enter opens. The keys act on the selection if there is one, otherwise on the tile the frame sits on. Colour labels can now also be set with 6-9 in full screen. The shift-click UNITES, it does not replace: a file manager throws away everything outside the range, and when sorting photos one only notices that loss by the smaller number in the bar. Valid in all four grids: timeline, calendar year, album, search.

Recognised text becomes readable. Text recognition has been running for a long time and puts its result into the database. It was used in exactly one place: as a filter in the search. In the test library 2,406 of 7,988 shots carried a text nobody could read. It now appears in the info panel as a selectable block with a button to copy it. And in the viewer a new symbol shows WHERE in the picture which text sits - tapping a box copies exactly that line. The boxes were always produced by the recognition and were simply discarded until now. For existing photos a run of the text recognition in the background tasks fetches them; shots without text are left out.

Faces get out of the program - and in. A grown library quickly holds thousands of recognised faces and a few dozen names. That is the most expensive handwork in it, and until now it could neither leave the program nor reach it. Sidecars, export and the unencrypted backup now write the named faces as MWG-RS regions - the format in which Lightroom, digiKam and PhotoPrism exchange names for picture locations. Reading works the other way round: imported regions are matched to the program's own faces by area overlap, and only nameless ones get a name. An assignment already made is never overwritten. In addition, reading now also covers embedded XMP when no .xmp file sits beside the photo. Everything arriving that way from Lightroom or digiKam used to arrive without keywords, without rating and without names - and the file did not show it.

Measure sharpness where the face is. The blur value applied to the whole picture. A portrait with a soft face in front of sharp foliage passes that test easily - and when culling that is exactly the shot one wants to discard. Every recognised person now gets its own sharpness value, computed on the crop that is stored anyway. When culling, a marker appears in the bar if even the SHARPEST face of a shot is too soft; in a group picture someone at the back is almost always soft, and that is no reason to throw the picture away. The threshold is not guessed but measured on 1,625 real crops. For existing faces there is a separate background task - it needs about two milliseconds per face and does not have to decode a single photo again.

One sentence instead of twenty switches. The search knows two dozen criteria. Whoever knows they exist finds everything with them; whoever does not types a sentence and gets an image search that understands nothing of "5 stars". Typed into the search field, what can be read is now read: rating, colour label, photos or videos, favourites, dates ("2019", "last year", "summer 2019", "in July") and everything that exists as a person, keyword, camera or place in the library. What was understood appears as chips below the field - with a button that undoes the interpretation and searches literally again. What was NOT understood stays untouched and goes to the image search as before; the search is therefore in no case worse than before. Only what is typed by hand is interpreted: a saved smart album runs on unchanged, otherwise it would find something else tomorrow than today. Negations, conjunctions and comparisons are deliberately not understood - a half-understood "without" would be worse than none: it would deliver the opposite without the result list showing it.

Find sensor dust. Removing it has long existed - LaMa and the healing brush. What was missing is the finding. Under Tools, Find sensor dust, a sample spread over the whole period of one camera's shots is examined and whatever keeps appearing in the same place is reported. That repetition is the core: a single dark dot can be anything - a bird, a pebble. Dust differs in that it does not move. In the test library the run over three series of forty shots each found NO sensor dust. That this is down to the sensors and not the detection is proven: on an artificially soiled picture it finds both planted grains in the right place.

On updating: unpack the archive, drag the app into place, start it. Same identifier, same library. The database is lifted from version 59 to 61 on first start - two additional columns, the contents stay unchanged. The step was tried on three grown libraries. Two background tasks are new after the switch and are worth a run: text recognition (fetches the locations in the picture) and face sharpness.

Sechs Punkte aus dem Vergleich mit den Nachbarprogrammen - und der wichtigste davon kam nicht aus dem Vergleich, sondern aus der eigenen Bibliothek. Die Datenbank geht von Fassung 59 auf 61; die Migration laeuft beim ersten Start von selbst.

Sterne vergeben, ohne 200 Mal zu klicken. Bewertung und Farbmarke gibt es seit vielen Fassungen. Beim Nachzaehlen in einer gewachsenen Bibliothek mit 7.988 Aufnahmen standen dort null Bewertungen und null Farbmarken. Der Grund lag nicht an der Funktion, sondern am Weg dorthin: Das Raster kannte keine einzige Taste, die Auswahl begann mit einem langen Druck - einer Fingergeste -, und eine Bereichsauswahl gab es ueberhaupt nicht. Jetzt: Umschalt-Klick nimmt alles zwischen der zuletzt angeklickten und der neuen Kachel dazu; Strg- bzw. Command-Klick schaltet eine einzelne Kachel um; die Pfeiltasten bewegen einen sichtbaren Rahmen durchs Raster, Umschalt+Pfeil zieht die Auswahl mit; 0-5 setzt die Bewertung, 6-9 die Farbmarke, F den Favoriten, Escape leert, Eingabe oeffnet. Die Tasten wirken auf die Auswahl, wenn es eine gibt - sonst auf die Kachel, auf der der Rahmen steht. Farbmarken lassen sich jetzt auch im Vollbild ueber 6-9 setzen. Der Umschalt-Klick vereinigt, er ersetzt nicht: Ein Dateimanager wirft alles ausserhalb des Bereichs weg, und beim Aussuchen von Fotos bemerkt man diesen Verlust erst an der kleiner gewordenen Zahl in der Leiste. Gueltig in allen vier Rastern: Zeitleiste, Kalenderjahr, Album, Suche.

Der erkannte Text wird lesbar. Die Texterkennung laeuft seit Langem und legt ihr Ergebnis in die Datenbank. Benutzt wurde es an genau einer Stelle: als Filter in der Suche. In der Pruefbibliothek trugen 2.406 von 7.988 Aufnahmen einen Text, den niemand lesen konnte. In der Info-Ansicht steht er jetzt als markierbarer Block, mit einem Knopf zum Kopieren. Und im Betrachter laesst sich ueber ein neues Symbol einblenden, wo im Bild welcher Text steht - ein Tipp auf einen Kasten legt genau diese Zeile in die Zwischenablage. Die Kaesten fielen bei der Erkennung immer schon an und wurden bisher weggeworfen. Fuer vorhandene Fotos holt sie ein Lauf der Texterkennung in den Hintergrundaufgaben nach; Aufnahmen ohne Text bleiben aussen vor.

Gesichter kommen aus dem Programm heraus - und hinein. In einer gewachsenen Bibliothek stecken schnell tausende erkannte Gesichter und ein paar Dutzend Namen. Das ist die teuerste Handarbeit darin, und sie konnte das Programm bisher weder verlassen noch erreichen. Beipackzettel, Export und die unverschluesselte Sicherung schreiben die benannten Gesichter jetzt als MWG-RS-Regionen - das Format, in dem Lightroom, digiKam und PhotoPrism Namen zu Bildstellen austauschen. Beim Einlesen geht es andersherum: Eingelesene Regionen werden ueber die Flaechenueberdeckung den eigenen Gesichtern zugeordnet, und nur noch namenlose bekommen einen Namen. Eine bereits vergebene Zuordnung wird nie ueberschrieben. Dazu liest das Einlesen jetzt auch eingebettetes XMP, wenn kein .xmp daneben liegt. Alles, was so aus Lightroom oder digiKam kommt, kam bisher ohne Schlagwoerter, ohne Bewertung und ohne Namen an - und man sah es der Datei nicht an.

Schaerfe dort messen, wo das Gesicht ist. Der Unschaerfewert galt bisher fuer das ganze Bild. Ein Portraet mit unscharfem Gesicht vor scharfem Laub besteht diese Pruefung muehelos - und beim Sichten ist genau das die Aufnahme, die man aussortieren will. Jede erkannte Person bekommt jetzt einen eigenen Schaerfewert, gerechnet auf dem Ausschnitt, der ohnehin gespeichert ist. Beim Sichten erscheint ein Zeichen in der Leiste, wenn auch das schaerfste Gesicht einer Aufnahme zu weich ist; auf einem Gruppenbild ist hinten fast immer jemand unscharf, und das ist kein Grund, das Bild wegzuwerfen. Die Schwelle ist nicht geschaetzt, sondern an 1.625 echten Ausschnitten gemessen. Fuer vorhandene Gesichter gibt es eine eigene Hintergrundaufgabe - sie braucht rund zwei Millisekunden je Gesicht und muss kein Foto neu dekodieren.

Ein Satz statt zwanzig Schalter. Die Suche kennt zwei Dutzend Kriterien. Wer weiss, dass es sie gibt, findet damit alles; wer es nicht weiss, tippt einen Satz und bekommt eine Bildsuche, die von "5 Sterne" nichts versteht. Ins Suchfeld getippt, wird jetzt gelesen, was sich lesen laesst: Bewertung, Farbmarke, Fotos oder Videos, Favoriten, Zeitangaben ("2019", "letztes Jahr", "Sommer 2019", "im Juli") und alles, was als Person, Schlagwort, Kamera oder Ort in der Bibliothek steht. Was verstanden wurde, steht als Marken unter dem Feld - mit einem Knopf, der die Deutung zuruecknimmt und wieder woertlich sucht. Was nicht verstanden wurde, bleibt unangetastet stehen und geht wie bisher an die Bildsuche; die Suche ist damit in keinem Fall schlechter als vorher. Gedeutet wird nur, was von Hand ins Feld getippt wurde: Ein gespeichertes intelligentes Album laeuft unveraendert weiter, sonst faende es morgen etwas anderes als heute. Verneinungen, Verknuepfungen und Vergleiche versteht der Leser bewusst nicht - ein halbverstandenes "ohne" waere schlimmer als gar keines: Es lieferte das Gegenteil, ohne dass man es der Trefferliste ansieht.

Sensorstaub finden. Das Wegrechnen gibt es laengst - LaMa und der Reparaturpinsel. Was fehlte, ist das Finden. Unter Werkzeuge, Sensorstaub suchen, wird eine ueber den ganzen Zeitraum verteilte Stichprobe der Aufnahmen einer Kamera untersucht und gemeldet, was immer wieder an derselben Stelle auftaucht. Diese Wiederholung ist der Kern: Ein einzelner dunkler Punkt kann alles sein - ein Vogel, ein Kiesel. Staub unterscheidet sich dadurch, dass er sich nicht bewegt. In der Pruefbibliothek fand der Lauf ueber drei Serien zu je vierzig Aufnahmen keinen Sensorstaub. Dass das an den Sensoren liegt und nicht an der Erkennung, ist belegt: Auf einem kuenstlich verschmutzten Bild findet sie beide eingezeichneten Koerner an der richtigen Stelle.

Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek. Die Datenbank wird beim ersten Start von Fassung 59 auf 61 gehoben - zwei zusaetzliche Spalten, der Bestand bleibt unveraendert. Der Schritt wurde an drei gewachsenen Bibliotheken erprobt. Zwei Hintergrundaufgaben sind nach dem Umstieg neu und lohnen einen Lauf: Texterkennung (holt die Stellen im Bild nach) und Gesichtsschaerfe.
Journeys and activities can now be corrected after the fact, there is a new type and room for your own - plus two measured optimisations. No schema change; the database stays at version 59.

Changing the photos of a journey or activity. The assignment was made ONCE and then stayed as it was: by the detection at a gap of ninety minutes, or when creating one by hand over its period. Both are often right and not always - the photo from the evening before sometimes belongs, the one from the lunch break sometimes does not. There is now a button for it in both the journey and the activity. Behind it a grid with check marks, for both directions: adding and removing are the same question. The period is only the default of the view, not its boundary - under "All photos" one from outside can be taken in. What is not on screen stays untouched: a line says how many of the selected ones are currently not visible. And the period of the journey is carried along as soon as the photos change.

Walk - and everything else. "Walk" is new in the list of types. It is not guessed: the calculated distance is a lower bound (straight lines between photos, breaks in between), so a short measured distance does not prove a short way. Below the list there is now "New type". Whatever is typed there appears in the list from then on - on every activity and in every picker. Typing "Hike" gives you the built-in one; two entries of the same name would be no order at all. A type of your own lives as long as an activity carries it; whoever moves the last one away will not find the name in the list any more - it can simply be typed again.

Two optimisations, both measured. The grid decodes in steps. A grid divides the available space evenly, so the tile width changes with every single point of window width. Every intermediate step of dragging the window edge used to be its own size in the image cache - and therefore a fresh decode for every visible tile. One decode to 148 points takes 0.68 ms; window widths from 1000 to 1400 produced 21 different sizes, in steps of 32 they produce one. With fifty visible tiles that was around 0.7 seconds of decoding work for a single drag of the window edge.

The start is a third of a second shorter. The place directory (cities1000.txt, 31 MB) was read before the first frame - a measured 376 ms for something the first frame does not need. It now loads alongside; the import waits for it, the views do not.
On updating: unpack the archive, drag the app into place, start it. Same identifier, same library, no schema step.
Reisen und Aktivitaeten lassen sich jetzt nachbessern, es gibt eine neue Art und Platz fuer eigene - und zwei gemessene Optimierungen. Kein neues Schema; die Datenbank bleibt auf Fassung 59.

Die Fotos einer Reise oder Aktivitaet aendern. Die Zuordnung entstand bisher EINMAL und blieb dann, wie sie war: bei der Erkennung an einer Luecke von anderthalb Stunden, beim Anlegen von Hand ueber den Zeitraum. Beides trifft oft und nicht immer - das Foto vom Vorabend gehoert manchmal dazu, das aus der Mittagspause manchmal nicht. In der Reise und in der Aktivitaet steht jetzt ein Knopf dafuer. Dahinter ein Raster mit Haekchen, fuer beides: Hinzufuegen und Entfernen sind dieselbe Frage. Der Zeitraum ist dabei nur die Voreinstellung der Ansicht, nicht ihre Grenze - ueber "Alle Fotos" laesst sich eines von ausserhalb dazunehmen. Was nicht im Bild steht, bleibt unangetastet: Eine Zeile sagt, wie viele der Gewaehlten gerade nicht zu sehen sind. Und der Zeitraum der Reise wird nachgefuehrt, sobald sich die Fotos aendern.

Spaziergang - und alles andere. "Spaziergang" ist neu in der Liste der Arten. Geraten wird er nicht: Die gerechnete Strecke ist eine Untergrenze (Luftlinie zwischen Fotos, Pausen dazwischen), eine kurze gemessene Strecke belegt also keinen kurzen Weg. Darunter steht jetzt "Neue Art". Was dort eingetippt wird, steht danach in der Liste - bei jeder Aktivitaet und in jedem Auswahlfenster. Wer "Wanderung" eintippt, bekommt die mitgelieferte; zwei Eintraege desselben Namens waeren keine Ordnung. Eine eigene Art lebt, solange eine Aktivitaet sie traegt; wer die letzte davon umtraegt, findet den Namen nicht mehr in der Auswahl - er laesst sich genauso wieder eintippen.

Zwei Optimierungen, beide gemessen. Das Raster dekodiert in Stufen. Ein Raster teilt den vorhandenen Platz gleichmaessig auf; die Kachelbreite aendert sich damit mit jedem Punkt Fensterbreite. Jeder Zwischenschritt eines Ziehens am Fensterrand war bisher eine eigene Groesse im Bildspeicher - und damit fuer jede sichtbare Kachel ein neuer Dekodiervorgang. Ein Dekodiervorgang auf 148 Punkte dauert 0,68 ms; die Fensterbreiten 1000 bis 1400 ergaben 21 verschiedene Groessen, in Stufen zu 32 ergeben sie eine. Bei fuenfzig sichtbaren Kacheln waren das rund 0,7 Sekunden Dekodierarbeit fuer ein einziges Ziehen am Fensterrand.

Der Start ist eine Drittelsekunde kuerzer. Das Ortsverzeichnis (cities1000.txt, 31 MB) wurde vor dem ersten Bild gelesen - gemessene 376 ms fuer etwas, das das erste Bild nicht braucht. Es laedt jetzt nebenher; der Import wartet darauf, die Ansichten nicht.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemaschritt.
Six things one wanted to do and could not - and a note that stayed lying next to the vault. No schema change; the database stays at version 59.

Who is in this photo? The info panel lists the named people as a row of heads, but it does not say WHICH head in the picture is whose - and it keeps quiet about the unnamed ones entirely. Frames existed only in the face editor, reachable solely through a right-click menu. Now there is a button in the toolbar: green means named (tapping leads to the person), orange means unnamed (tapping asks for the name), grey means set aside. Naming used to work only through "the first unnamed face in this photo" - in a group shot one named somebody at random.

The family tree can be moved. Dragging pans, swiping zooms, and beside it stand three buttons: closer, further, Show all. A tree with in-laws is wider than any window; until now one never got to see it whole, and without scrollbars - trackpad, Magic Mouse - not even to its edge. It also opens in the right place now: first the whole tree is centred, and only if the plate of the focus person would fall outside does the view move to that plate. Before, it began at the top left corner, that is at some great-grandfather.

Two maps could not be zoomed at all. The world map of the journeys and the family places had neither zoom buttons nor the swipe zoom. With a mouse without a wheel there was NO zoom there, and with a wheel no hint that it was possible. Both now carry the same bar as the large map.

The grandchildren were missing. The tree reached three generations up and ONE down. Grandchildren, great-grandchildren and the children of nephews and nieces are now included - as far down as up. On a plate carrying a marker both above and below, the relationship line lay half over the name: three lines need 56.6 points, the plate has 67, and two markers of thirteen each make 82.6. They now sit as a mark on the edge and cost no line.

Larger system font. Above 1.21 times the system font size EVERY plate overflowed: the text followed the setting, the plate stayed at its 132 by 108 points. A plate cannot be stretched - so the whole tree now grows with it.

The note beside the vault. Tools, Write XMP sidecars places an .xmp file next to every photo with description, keywords, rating and location, so that Lightroom and darktable can read them. When locking a photo, that file stayed in plain text - the original became ciphertext, the note beside it remained readable. Exactly what the locked folder protects against. On permanent deletion it stayed behind as well, forever: the database row was gone, and nobody knew of the file any more. Both had the same cause - the same list of file kinds, maintained by hand in three places. It now exists once. Note for existing libraries: notes left behind by earlier versions do not vanish by themselves. Whoever has locked photos and uses XMP sidecars should unlock them once and lock them again; then they are encrypted along with the rest.
A way to the life events. The life events of a person existed only in the menu of their plate in the family tree. Whoever opened a person did not find them. Now there is a button in their toolbar.
On updating: unpack the archive, drag the app into place, start it. Same identifier, same library, no schema step.
Sechs Dinge, die man tun wollte und nicht konnte - und ein Zettel, der neben dem Tresor liegen blieb. Kein neues Schema; die Datenbank bleibt auf Fassung 59.

Wer ist auf diesem Foto? Die Info-Ansicht zaehlt die benannten Personen als Reihe von Koepfen auf. Sie sagt aber nicht, WELCHER Kopf im Bild welcher ist - und die unbenannten Gesichter verschweigt sie ganz. Rahmen gab es nur in der Gesichts-Bearbeitung, erreichbar allein ueber ein Rechtsklick-Menue. Jetzt liegt in der Leiste ein Knopf: gruen benannt (Tippen fuehrt zur Person), orange unbenannt (Tippen fragt nach dem Namen), grau beiseitegelegt. Benennen ging bisher nur ueber "das erste unbenannte Gesicht dieses Fotos" - bei einer Gruppenaufnahme benannte man damit blind irgendwen.

Der Stammbaum laesst sich bewegen. Ziehen verschiebt, Wischen zoomt, und daneben stehen drei Knoepfe: naeher heran, weiter weg, Ganz zeigen. Ein Baum mit angeheirateter Verwandtschaft ist breiter als jedes Fenster; bisher bekam man ihn nie ganz zu sehen, und ohne Rollbalken - Tastflaeche, Magic Mouse - nicht einmal an seinen Rand. Und er schlaegt an der richtigen Stelle auf: Erst wird der ganze Baum eingemittet, und nur wenn das Schild der Mitte dabei aus dem Bild fiele, rueckt der Ausschnitt auf dieses Schild. Vorher begann er in der linken oberen Ecke, also bei irgendeinem Urgrossvater.

Zwei Karten liessen sich gar nicht zoomen. Die Weltkarte der Reisen und die Familienorte hatten weder Zoomknoepfe noch den Wisch-Zoom. An einer Maus ohne Rad war dort KEIN Zoom moeglich, und mit Rad gab es keinen Hinweis, dass es ginge. Beide haben jetzt dieselbe Leiste wie die grosse Karte.

Die Enkel fehlten. Der Baum reichte drei Generationen hinauf und EINE hinab. Enkel, Urenkel und die Kinder der Neffen kommen dazu - so weit hinunter wie hinauf. Auf einem Schild, das oben und unten ein Mehrzeichen trug, lag die Verhaeltnisangabe halb ueber dem Namen: Drei Zeilen brauchen 56,6 Punkte, die Tafel hat 67, und mit zwei Zeichen zu je dreizehn werden daraus 82,6. Sie liegen jetzt als Marke an der Kante und kosten keine Zeile.

Groessere Systemschrift. Ab dem 1,21-fachen lief JEDES Schild ueber: Die Schrift folgte der Einstellung, das Schild blieb bei seinen 132 auf 108 Punkten. Ein Schild laesst sich nicht dehnen - jetzt waechst der ganze Baum mit.

Der Beipackzettel neben dem Tresor. Werkzeuge, XMP-Beilagen schreiben legt neben jedes Foto eine .xmp-Datei mit Beschreibung, Schlagwoertern, Bewertung und Ort, damit Lightroom und darktable sie lesen koennen. Beim Sperren blieb sie im Klartext liegen - das Original wurde zu Chiffrat, der Zettel daneben war weiter lesbar. Genau das, wovor der gesperrte Ordner schuetzt. Beim endgueltigen Loeschen blieb er ebenfalls liegen, fuer immer: Die Datenbankzeile war weg, und niemand wusste mehr von der Datei. Beides hatte dieselbe Ursache - dieselbe Liste von Dateiarten, an drei Stellen von Hand gepflegt. Sie steht jetzt einmal da. Fuer vorhandene Bibliotheken: Zettel, die vor dieser Fassung liegen geblieben sind, verschwinden nicht von selbst. Wer Fotos gesperrt hat und XMP-Beilagen benutzt, sperrt sie einmal auf und wieder zu - dann sind sie mitverschluesselt.
Ein Weg zum Lebenslauf. Den Lebenslauf einer Person gab es nur im Menue ihres Schildes im Stammbaum. Wer eine Person aufschlug, fand ihn nicht. Jetzt steht ein Knopf in ihrer Leiste.
Zum Aktualisieren: Archiv auspacken, die App an ihren Platz ziehen, starten. Dieselbe Kennung, dieselbe Bibliothek, kein Schemaschritt.
The family tree now shows how people stand to ONE ANOTHER - as a tree with branches instead of rows by role. No schema change; the database stays at version 59.

"Mother of brother-in-law Michael" instead of "related by marriage". For brothers-in-law, parents-in-law, stepchildren and second cousins Photo Vault has long had a word. For everything else it had exactly one: "related by marriage" - the same answer for one's own brother-in-law's mother as for the cousin of an uncle's second wife. Where the language has no word, the WAY there is now described: Michael is the brother-in-law, Petra the mother of brother-in-law Michael, Klaus his brother. The detour runs over exactly one intermediate person, and that person must have a name of their own. "The grandfather of the father of the brother-in-law" stays "related by marriage" - it explains less than nothing.

The tree has branches. Until now relatives stood in rows by role: one line of parents, one of siblings, one headed "brothers- and sisters-in-law". A row cannot say WHICH sister a brother-in-law belongs to. Now a person and their partner form a household, and the line of descent hangs on the individual person. The brother-in-law therefore stands visibly beside his wife - and his parents hang from HIM, not from you. One generation further is shown than before: great-grandparents, the partner's grandparents, and both the parents AND the siblings of the in-laws. If a band no longer fits the sheet, a line says how many households are missing; leaving them out in silence would be the worst of both.

And it looks like a tree. Golden tapering branches on a dark ground, name plates with portraits, the family name at the foot of the trunk. Whoever works in light mode gets bronze on parchment - not the same golden tones on white, where they lose all footing. Every plate carries name, relationship and dates. Tapping moves that person to the centre; the button at the top right opens the same menu as before. Honestly: these are well-kept branches with a few flourishes, not the dense baroque of a printed canvas. What is here and missing there: the branches mean something.
A board to hang up. Menu, Ornamental tree as PDF draws the same tree at three times the size onto an A3 sheet - without portraits, as on any printed pedigree.

The first font of its own. Until now every typeface came from the system and therefore looked different on macOS, Linux and Windows. For a sheet on the wall that is precisely the point. EB Garamond now ships for the plates and Great Vibes for the family name, both under the SIL Open Font License. Their licence texts can now also be read: Settings, Licences shows them together with those of every library in use. That overview did not exist before.
On updating: unpack the archive, drag the app into place, start it. Same identifier, same library, no schema step.
Der Stammbaum zeigt jetzt, wie die Leute ZUEINANDER stehen - als Baum mit Aesten statt als Reihen nach Rolle. Kein neues Schema; die Datenbank bleibt auf Fassung 59.

"Mutter von Schwager Michael" statt "angeheiratet". Fuer Schwager, Schwiegereltern, Stiefkinder und Cousins zweiten Grades hatte Photo Vault laengst ein Wort. Fuer alles andere hatte es genau eines: "angeheiratet" - dieselbe Auskunft fuer die Mutter des eigenen Schwagers wie fuer den Vetter der zweiten Frau eines Onkels. Wo die Sprache kein Wort hat, wird jetzt der WEG beschrieben: Michael ist der Schwager, Petra die Mutter von Schwager Michael, Klaus dessen Bruder. Der Umweg geht ueber genau eine Zwischenperson, und die muss selbst einen Namen haben. "Der Grossvater des Vaters des Schwagers" bleibt "angeheiratet" - das erklaert weniger als gar nichts.

Der Baum hat Aeste. Bisher standen die Verwandten in Reihen nach Rolle: eine Zeile Eltern, eine Zeile Geschwister, eine Zeile "Schwager und Schwaegerin".
